title: Actionable self-help advice items
description: This latent fires on generic, prescriptive advice statements—typically imperative or suggestion-style sentences (often in bulleted or numbered self-help/advice-column text) that recommend a concrete action, coping strategy, or resource for improving one's life, finances, career, relationships, or wellbeing (e.g., 'join clubs,' 'try online courses,' 'exercise releases endorphins,' 'consolidate your debts'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic recommendation sentences that name a practical step or benefit ('This can simplify your payments,' 'Attend networking events,' 'Practice mindfulness'), especially those following a template of listing options or explaining a mechanism of benefit. It does NOT activate strongly on purely emotional validation statements, rhetorical questions, narrative/dialogue lines, or abstract reflective commentary that lacks a concrete suggested action or resource, even if topically related to self-improvement or relationships.

title: Validating affirmation of self-worth and self-care
description: This latent fires on direct, second-person affirmations that validate the reader's worth, feelings, or choices and affirm their right to prioritize their own well-being ('You are worthy...', 'Remember, you deserve...', 'You're taking care of yourself, and that's what matters'). It activates most strongly on formulaic, therapeutic-sounding reassurance statements that combine a validating claim about the person's character or situation with permission-giving language around self-care, boundaries, or emotional needs, often beginning with 'You are/You're' or 'Remember'. It is weaker or absent on sentences that give practical advice, describe other people's behavior, pose questions, or discuss situational facts without an explicit affirming/validating address to the reader (e.g., advice to 'reflect on' something, descriptions of a third party's autonomy, or neutral statements about relationships), even if those sentences share vocabulary like 'well-being' or 'prioritize'.

title: Structured listicle formatting in advice responses
description: This latent fires on the scaffolding of AI-generated advice/listicle text: bare numeric list markers ('1.', '2.', '3.'), bolded concept headers followed by a colon and explanation (e.g. 'Projection**: Accusing you of...'), and templated clarifying-question phrases used to request more detail (e.g. 'Can you please provide more information about the error, such as:'). It activates most strongly on these formulaic organizational and elicitation cues rather than on the substantive content of the advice itself, and also fires more weakly on other sentences within such structured advice responses (options, suggestions, considerations) that share the same list-like, enumerative register. It would not activate on plain narrative or conversational prose that lacks list markers, bolded terms, or a request-for-more-information template, even if the topic (e.g. relationship advice, tech troubleshooting) is similar.

title: Validating, reassuring advice-column affirmations
description: This latent fires on supportive, validating statements typical of relationship/advice-column responses -- affirmations like 'you deserve respect,' 'you did the best you could,' 'don't worry about it,' and 'use this as an opportunity to learn and grow.' It activates on sentences that reassure the reader, affirm their worth or effort, normalize their feelings/situation, or frame a conflict as a growth opportunity, often addressed directly to 'you' in a therapeutic or advice-giving register. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, procedural instructions without emotional validation (e.g., 'check the pool's rules'), or descriptive/narrative sentences that lack this reassuring, second-person affirming tone, even if they occur in the same advice-giving context.

title: Evaluative validation of the person's feelings or actions
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic evaluative statements that render a verdict on a situation, feeling, or behavior described in advice-column-style text (e.g., 'That's not okay', 'That's a reasonable expectation', 'You had every right to feel upset', 'Your reaction was also unkind'). These are typically brief declarative sentences that validate, normalize, criticize, or morally assess the reader's or another party's conduct/emotions, often serving as a discourse pivot between describing a situation and offering advice. It activates most strongly on terse, standalone judgment sentences ('That's a big deal', 'That's not healthy or respectful') and also, more weakly, on longer sentences that embed the same evaluative/validating move within advice or explanation. It does NOT activate on purely descriptive narrative statements, factual/informational content (e.g., biological facts, procedural steps like 'set a specific day'), or neutral suggestions that lack an explicit judgment or validation of feelings/behavior.
